description: Negative examples and the failure each one must produce. A negative example that fails for the wrong reason is as much a bug as one that passes, so CI matches the reported error rather than only the exit code.

cases.rationale: kind is declared_egress_point, which forces source to be declared. This exercises the conditional block, not just field presence.

cases.violates: operation spelling is fixed by the event contract
cases.rationale: The reconciliation join compares this field against the operation a runtime hook recorded, and the hook writes lower case by contract. A finding spelled Chat.Completions.Create would validate as a string, join against nothing, and report a code point that did run as dormant. The pattern is what turns that silent mismatch into a rejection.
A report without a coverage statement must be rejected at schema level. This is the honest coverage principle made unbreakable rather than merely documented.

cases.violates: the run must say which rule set decided it
cases.rationale: Every other field here counts something the scan could not see. This one names the detectors that decided what counted as seen at all, and it is required for the same reason the block is: a report that omits it reads as if the shipped detectors produced it. An operator can pass --rules at a narrow directory, get a clean PASS, and archive it; six months later nobody can tell that run apart from one made with the set we ship. rule_set_hash pins the content of the rules and says nothing about where they came from, so leaving the field optional would make the honest answer the one a producer has to remember rather than one the schema enforces.

cases.violates: payload shape may not carry content
cases.rationale: The hook records structure, never content. A raw_body field would turn an observation tool into a copy of the data it was deployed to protect, so the schema refuses the field outright rather than trusting every caller to leave it out.

cases.violates: the observation window is a duration, never a wall clock stamp
cases.rationale: A stamp in this field would put a clock value into the one number every dormant_egress_point finding rests on, and two runs over the same observations would then reconcile differently. The field is also what tells a reader whether the hook was watching for ten minutes or ten milliseconds, so a string that merely looks temporal must be rejected rather than parsed leniently by whichever reader gets there first.

cases.violates: a flow may not carry payload bytes
cases.rationale: The sensor observes destinations, not contents. A field for payload bytes would turn the component deployed to find leaks into one, so the schema refuses it rather than relying on every implementation to leave it out.

Until schema version 1.2 the value proxy failed here exactly as proxy-admin does now: the enum listed four components and the proxy was not one of them, so the component that intercepts the traffic could not emit a contract shaped finding at all. Adding proxy to the enum is what closed that gap, and this example is the proof that the enum is still a gate rather than a comment: a component name nobody registered is rejected, not carried through into a report as if some detector had produced it.

cases.violates: the measurement record may not carry a value
cases.rationale: The absolute constraint of this contract is that the record carries types, counts, rungs and durations, never a value. A field holding alias strings or raw entity text would turn the component built to keep data inside into the thing that writes it to disk on every request, so additionalProperties refuses the field outright instead of trusting each producer to leave it out.

cases.violates: entity type identifiers are a closed set
cases.rationale: A rule naming a type no detector produces cannot mask anything. Accepting it silently is the worst outcome available: the operator reads the policy, believes identity numbers are blocked, and the data leaves unmasked. Fail closed at load is the only honest answer, and the three load errors in proxy-policy.md section 7 are kept distinguishable so the message tells the operator which mistake they made.

cases.violates: unknown keys are rejected, and P-0 may not be relaxed by one
cases.rationale: Two rules meet in this example. Unknown keys stop the load because a silently ignored key is a setting the operator believes is in force. This particular key is also the one ADR-010 named and refused: no key may relax P-0 into generating an identifier that could belong to a real person. A closed property set is what keeps that refusal from depending on review.

cases.violates: mode values are a closed set
cases.rationale: redact is not a mode. A loader that shrugged and fell back to the default would answer a request to remove data by masking it under a different rule than the operator asked for. The error points at the offending path so this failure is distinguishable from the unknown type and unknown key cases, which is what proxy-policy.md section 7 requires of the three.

cases.violates: every dictionary entry must map to an entity type
cases.rationale: An entry with no type has no alias generator behind it. Loading it would produce a match at scan time and a failure at alias time, in the middle of a request that has already been accepted; the same value would then be either dropped or passed through depending on error handling. Requiring the mapping at load turns a mid request failure into a startup failure.

cases.violates: a proxy measurement must declare the masking profile it was taken under
cases.rationale: performance-budgets.md states that a proxy latency measurement with no profile declared is invalid, because the two profiles answer to different budgets and their numbers may not share a series. Without the field a NER profile number lands next to core profile numbers and the trend line reads as a regression that never happened, or a real one hides behind it. The schema enforces what the prose asserted.

cases.violates: a server name may only exist where the handshake showed one
cases.rationale: encrypted_client_hello measures a blind spot: the name was genuinely unavailable. A record that carries a name anyway contradicts the field measuring the loss, and the contradiction would be read as data rather than as a broken producer. This is the honest coverage principle enforced by the validator instead of by review.
